True Statement: There are more than 20,000 species of ants, 3,00,000 species of beetles, 28,000 species of fishes and nearly 20,000 species of orchids.

False 1: Biodiversity is the term popularised by the ecologist Robert May to describe combined diversity at all levels.

True Statement: According to IUCN (2004), the total number of plant and animal species described so far is slightly more than 1.5 million.

True Statement: A conservative and scientifically sound estimate made by Robert May places the global species diversity at about 7 million.

True Statement: More than 70 per cent of all the species recorded are animals, while plants (including algae, fungi, bryophytes, gymnosperms and angiosperms) comprise no more than 22 per cent of the total.

True Statement: Among animals, insects are the most species-rich taxonomic group, making up more than 70 per cent of the total.

True Statement: The number of fungi species in the world is more than the combined total of the species of fishes, amphibians, reptiles and mammals.

True Statement: Although India has only 2.4 per cent of the world's land area, its share of the global species diversity is an impressive 8.1 per cent.

True Statement: India is one of the 12 mega diversity countries of the world.

True Statement: Nearly 45,000 species of plants and twice as many of animals have been recorded from India.

True Statement: Species diversity decreases as we move away from the equator towards the poles.

True Statement: Colombia (located near the equator) has nearly 1,400 species of birds, while New York (41°N) has 105 species and Greenland (71°N) only 56 species.

True Statement: India has more than 1,200 species of birds.

True Statement: The largely tropical Amazonian rain forest in South America has the greatest biodiversity on earth — home to more than 40,000 species of plants, 3,000 of fishes, 1,300 of birds, 427 of mammals, 427 of amphibians, 378 of reptiles and more than 1,25,000 invertebrates.

False 2: The Amazonian rain forest is home to more than 40,000 species of plants and 3,000 of birds (not fishes).

True Statement: Tropical latitudes have remained relatively undisturbed for millions of years and thus had a long evolutionary time for species diversification, unlike temperate regions subjected to frequent glaciations.
False 1: Tropical latitudes were subjected to frequent glaciations, reducing evolutionary time for species diversification.
False 2: Temperate regions remained undisturbed for millions of years, giving them more evolutionary time for diversification.

True Statement: Tropical environments are less seasonal, relatively more constant and predictable, which promotes niche specialisation and leads to greater species diversity.
False 1: Tropical environments are highly seasonal and unpredictable, which promotes greater species diversity.

True Statement: More solar energy is available in the tropics, which contributes to higher productivity and in turn to greater diversity.
False 1: Less solar energy is available in the tropics; their greater diversity is due solely to evolutionary time.

True Statement: Alexander von Humboldt observed that within a region, species richness increased with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit.
False 1: Robert May observed that species richness increased with increasing explored area, but only up to a limit.

True Statement: The species-area relationship for a wide variety of taxa turns out to be a rectangular hyperbola; on a logarithmic scale, the relationship becomes a straight line.
False 1: The species-area relationship turns out to be an exponential curve; on a logarithmic scale it remains a curve.
False 2: The species-area relationship is a straight line on both normal and logarithmic scales.

True Statement: In the species-area equation log S = log C + Z log A, Z is the slope of the line (regression coefficient) and C is the Y-intercept.
False 1: In the equation log S = log C + Z log A, C is the slope of the line and Z is the Y-intercept.

True Statement: The value of Z (slope) lies in the range of 0.1 to 0.2, regardless of the taxonomic group or the region.
False 1: The value of Z lies in the range of 0.6 to 1.2, regardless of the taxonomic group or the region.
False 2: The value of Z lies in the range of 0.3 to 0.5, regardless of the taxonomic group or region.

True Statement: For very large areas like entire continents, the slope of the species-area line is much steeper with Z values in the range of 0.6 to 1.2.

True Statement: For frugivorous (fruit-eating) birds and mammals in tropical forests of different continents, the slope is found to be 1.15.

True Statement: Communities with more species generally tend to be more stable than those with fewer species.
False 1: Communities with fewer species tend to be more stable than those with more species.

False 1: Robert May found that plots with more species showed less year-to-year variation in total biomass.
False 2: David Tilman found that plots with more species showed more year-to-year variation in total biomass.

True Statement: Tilman showed that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity.
False 1: Tilman showed that increased diversity contributed to lower productivity.
False 2: Edward Wilson showed that increased diversity contributed to higher productivity.

True Statement: Stanford ecologist Paul Ehrlich used the 'rivet popper hypothesis' to explain the importance of biodiversity.
False 1: David Tilman used the 'rivet popper hypothesis' to explain the importance of biodiversity.
False 2: Paul Ehrlich used the 'keystone species hypothesis' to explain the importance of biodiversity.

False 1: The colonisation of tropical Pacific Islands led to extinction of more than 500 species of native birds.

True Statement: The IUCN Red List (2004) documents the extinction of 784 species (including 338 vertebrates, 359 invertebrates and 87 plants) in the last 500 years.

True Statement: Examples of recent extinctions include the dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa), thylacine (Australia) and Steller's Sea Cow (Russia).
False 1: Examples of recent extinctions include the dodo (Africa), quagga (Mauritius) and thylacine (Australia).
False 2: Examples of recent extinctions include the dodo (Mauritius), quagga (Africa) and thylacine (New Zealand).

True Statement: The last twenty years alone have witnessed the disappearance of 27 species.
False 1: The last fifty years alone have witnessed the disappearance of 27 species.
False 2: The last twenty years have witnessed the disappearance of over 100 species.

True Statement: Presently, 12 per cent of all bird species, 23 per cent of all mammal species, 32 per cent of all amphibian species and 31 per cent of all gymnosperm species face the threat of extinction.
False 1: Presently, 23 per cent of all bird species and 12 per cent of all mammal species face the threat of extinction.
False 2: Presently, 12 per cent of all bird species, 23 per cent of mammal species, 23 per cent of amphibian species and 31 per cent of gymnosperm species face extinction.

True Statement: There were five episodes of mass extinction of species during the long history of life on earth before humans appeared.
False 1: There were three episodes of mass extinction during the long history of life on earth.
False 2: There were seven episodes of mass extinction during the long history of life on earth.

True Statement: Current species extinction rates are estimated to be 100 to 1,000 times faster than in pre-human times.
False 1: Current extinction rates are 10 to 100 times faster than in pre-human times.
False 2: Current extinction rates are 1,000 to 10,000 times faster than in pre-human times.

True Statement: If present trends continue, nearly half of all the species on earth might be wiped out within the next 100 years.
False 1: If present trends continue, nearly one-tenth of all species might be wiped out within the next 100 years.
False 2: If present trends continue, nearly half of all species might be wiped out within the next 50 years.

True Statement: Loss of biodiversity in a region may lead to: decline in plant production, lowered resistance to environmental perturbations, and increased variability in ecosystem processes.
False 1: Loss of biodiversity leads to increased plant production and greater resistance to environmental perturbations.
False 2: Loss of biodiversity leads only to decline in plant production, with no effect on ecosystem processes.

True Statement: Habitat loss and fragmentation is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction.
False 1: Over-exploitation is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction.
False 2: Alien species invasion is the most important cause driving animals and plants to extinction.

True Statement: Tropical rain forests once covered more than 14 per cent of the earth's land surface but now cover no more than 6 per cent.
False 1: Tropical rain forests once covered more than 20 per cent of the earth's land surface but now cover no more than 6 per cent.

True Statement: The Amazon rain forest is called the 'lungs of the planet'.
False 1: The Congo rain forest is called the 'lungs of the planet'.
False 2: The Amazon rain forest is called the 'heart of the planet'.

True Statement: The Amazon rain forest is being cut and cleared for cultivating soya beans or for conversion to grasslands for raising beef cattle.
False 1: The Amazon rain forest is being cut for cultivating rice and conversion to tea plantations.
False 2: The Amazon rain forest is cleared for mining operations and urban expansion only.

True Statement: The Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria in east Africa led to the extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish.
False 1: The Nile perch introduced into Lake Tanganyika led to extinction of more than 200 species of cichlid fish.
False 2: The Nile perch introduced into Lake Victoria led to extinction of more than 200 species of native catfish.

True Statement: Invasive weed species threatening native species include carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water hyacinth (Eicchornia).
False 1: Invasive weed species include carrot grass (Lantana), Parthenium and water hyacinth (Eicchornia).
False 2: Invasive weed species include carrot grass (Parthenium), Lantana and water fern (Salvinia).

True Statement: The African catfish Clarias gariepinus introduced for aquaculture purposes poses a threat to indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers.
False 1: The Nile perch introduced for aquaculture poses a threat to indigenous catfishes in Indian rivers.
False 2: The African catfish Clarias gariepinus poses a threat to indigenous cichlid fishes in Indian rivers.

True Statement: When a species becomes extinct, the plant and animal species associated with it in an obligatory way also become extinct — called co-extinction.
False 1: When a species becomes extinct, associated species adapt to other hosts and are not affected.
False 2: Co-extinction means two species become extinct simultaneously due to the same external cause, not due to dependence.

True Statement: Reasons for conserving biodiversity can be grouped into three categories: narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and ethical.
False 1: Reasons for conserving biodiversity can be grouped into two categories: utilitarian and ethical.
False 2: Reasons for conserving biodiversity can be grouped into three: narrowly utilitarian, broadly utilitarian and cultural.

True Statement: More than 25 per cent of the drugs currently sold in the market worldwide are derived from plants.
False 1: More than 10 per cent of the drugs currently sold in the market worldwide are derived from plants.
False 2: More than 50 per cent of the drugs currently sold in the market worldwide are derived from plants.

True Statement: 25,000 species of plants contribute to the traditional medicines used by native peoples around the world.
False 1: 5,000 species of plants contribute to the traditional medicines used by native peoples.

True Statement: The fast-dwindling Amazon forest is estimated to produce 20 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere through photosynthesis.
False 1: The Amazon forest is estimated to produce 50 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere.
False 2: The Amazon forest is estimated to produce 5 per cent of the total oxygen in the earth's atmosphere.

True Statement: Pollinators that provide the ecosystem service of pollination include bees, bumblebees, birds and bats.
False 1: Pollinators that provide the ecosystem service of pollination include only bees and butterflies.
False 2: Pollinators include bees, bumblebees, birds and bats; without them plants can still produce fruits and seeds.

True Statement: In situ conservation means conserving and protecting the whole ecosystem — saving the entire forest to save the tiger.
False 1: Ex situ conservation means conserving and protecting the whole ecosystem.
False 2: In situ conservation means taking animals out of their natural habitat and protecting them in special settings.

True Statement: Ex situ conservation is the desirable approach when an animal or plant is endangered and needs urgent measures to save it from extinction.
False 1: In situ conservation is the desirable approach when an animal or plant is endangered and needs urgent measures.
False 2: Ex situ conservation means protecting species within their natural habitat in protected areas.

True Statement: Initially 25 biodiversity hotspots were identified; subsequently nine more were added, bringing the total number of biodiversity hotspots in the world to 34.

True Statement: Biodiversity hotspots are regions with very high levels of species richness and high degree of endemism.

True Statement: Three biodiversity hotspots cover India's exceptionally high biodiversity regions: Western Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya.
False 1: Three hotspots cover India's biodiversity: Eastern Ghats and Sri Lanka, Indo-Burma and Himalaya.

True Statement: All the biodiversity hotspots put together cover less than 2 per cent of the earth's land area.

False 2: All biodiversity hotspots together cover about 5 per cent of the earth's land area.

True Statement: Strict protection of biodiversity hotspots could reduce the ongoing mass extinctions by almost 30 per cent.

True Statement: India has 14 biosphere reserves, 90 national parks and 448 wildlife sanctuaries.

True Statement: Sacred groves are found in Khasi and Jaintia Hills in Meghalaya, Aravalli Hills of Rajasthan, Western Ghat regions of Karnataka and Maharashtra, and Sarguja, Chanda and Bastar areas of Madhya Pradesh.

True Statement: In ex situ conservation, threatened animals and plants are taken out from their natural habitat and placed in special settings such as zoological parks, botanical gardens and wildlife safari parks.
False 1: In in situ conservation, threatened animals and plants are taken out from their natural habitat and placed in zoological parks and botanical gardens.

True Statement: Gametes of threatened species can be preserved in viable and fertile condition for long periods using cryopreservation techniques.

True Statement: Plants can be propagated using tissue culture methods in ex situ conservation.

True Statement: The Convention on Biological Diversity ('The Earth Summit') was held in Rio de Janeiro in 1992.

True Statement: 190 countries pledged their commitment to achieve by 2010 a significant reduction in the current rate of biodiversity loss.
